facts.text: Atmospheric plasma spraying was used to deposit an approximately 150 µm thick equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L.
The coated specimens were furnace-annealed for 2 h at 400, 550, 700, or 850 °C, with 550 °C selected as the optimum condition for corrosion testing.
Electrochemical corrosion testing was performed in 3.5 wt% H2SO4 using a saturated calomel reference electrode and a platinum counter electrode.
Hot-corrosion testing was conducted at 900 °C for ten 5 h cycles under three Na2SO4/NaCl salt mixtures containing 0, 10, or 20% V2O5.
Annealing at 550 °C produced a dense, refined coating microstructure with an average grain size near 15 µm, fewer voids, and retained major BCC and minor FCC phases.
The reported hardness increase was attributed to grain refinement and the major BCC phase impeding dislocation motion.
Corrosion protection was attributed to rapid formation of stable Al- and Cr-rich passive layers that restricted pit, crack, and sulphide-attack development.
Reported corrosion products included Cr2O3, Fe(OH)3, Cr(OH)3, and Co(OH)2, while molten chloride, sulphide, and vanadate species could eventually penetrate coating pores and cracks.
The 550 °C annealed coating exhibited greater microhardness than the annealed uncoated SS316L, whereas annealing at 700–850 °C reduced hardness relative to the 550 °C condition.
The 550 °C annealed coated specimen was reported to have 46% higher microhardness than annealed uncoated SS316L, and the average coated-sample hardness was 794 HV.

In 3.5 wt% H2SO4, the 550 °C annealed coating showed lower corrosion current and higher polarization resistance than both the as-sprayed coating and uncoated SS316L; its reported Icorr and Rp were 0.00374 µA and 1543.84 Ω·m².

During 900 °C hot corrosion, the 550 °C annealed coating reduced weight gain by 8.49–10.36% relative to the as-sprayed coating and by 42.09–44.25% relative to uncoated SS316L across the three salt mixtures.
